name: Eboo / Teke-Eboo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Raharimanantsoa, Ruth. 2017. The prosody of tense marking in Teke-Eboo, a Bantu B70 language of Congo-Brazzaville. Magister thesis (30 hp, AF2210, supervisor Laura Downing), Institutionen för språk och litteraturer, University of Gothenburg. 72 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/2077/52617(open access, GUPEA)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.3.1 p. 17; sec. 2.3.2 p. 18; sec. 6 p. 68 (= page); also abstract p. 2 and sec. 2.2 p. 9.
catalog_quote: [p.17] Thus Eboo has ‘stronger’ or more robust stem-initial syllables compared to other syllables, just like Kukuya, suggesting that a stem-initial stress accent is preventing weakening or deletion of the more complex forms such as NCG sequences and long nasal vowels which only occur in initial syllables. ... the larger set of consonants and consonant sequences in stem-initial position, many of which can be shown to have suffered deletion from second syllables and prefixes, does seem indicative of a stress accent ... [p.18] Eboo has a two way lexical tone contrast of H and L tones ... The mora is the tone bearing unit (TBU). ... the lexical tone contrast is marked on the stem-initial mora, giving it prominence as the stressed syllable ... [p.68] In both Teke varieties, it is difficult to find phonetic evidence of increased intensity on the initial syllable. There is nothing in the Eboo pitch graphs to indicate that stem-initial consonants or vowels are more intense, have a higher pitch, or are phonetically any different from consonants and vowels in other syllables. ... Since phonetic evidence for stress is hard to find, it may therefore be appropriate to rename Paulian’s stem-initial ‘stress accent’ in Kukuya, which is also attested in Eboo, as ‘stem-initial prominence’. There is little doubt that the stem-initial syllable has greater status or weight than other syllables which are prone to weakening and segmental loss.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Teke-Eboo-Nzikou (teke1278) is not in the catalog. the list of works with stress in the title had one title-hit, Raharimanantsoa 2017 (Gothenburg magister thesis, 72 pp.), already held by the project with a verified text; its handle was re-checked and is live. It is directly about this language and says Eboo, a two-tone (H/L) language, shows a fixed stem-initial 'stress accent' inferred from segmental asymmetry (full consonant/vowel inventory only in stem-initial syllables; lexical tone contrast on the stem-initial mora), but finds no intensity or pitch correlate and proposes calling it 'stem-initial prominence' (Lionnet 2017). This is the best first-hand statement for the language (no catalog record to supersede). Nothing new was downloaded; at was appended with this search of works with stress in the title note.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Teke-Eboo is a H/L tone language; word-level prominence ('stress accent' in Paulian's sense, re-labelled stem-initial prominence) falls on the stem-initial (root-initial) syllable, never on the noun-class or verbal prefix; the evidence is distributional (full consonant/vowel/NCG/long-vowel inventory only stem-initially, reduced inventories in later syllables and prefixes) and tonal (lexical tone contrast sits on the stem-initial mora; tone melodies run from one stressed stem-initial syllable to the next word's prefix); the author found no intensity or pitch correlate in her recordings.
new_statements.exceptions: None as to position; author notes stems longer than two syllables are mostly loans, reduplications or compounds and were excluded (p.14); a handful of nouns with fused prefix+stem (mwaana 'child') carry LHL on a long vowel (p.18). Caveat stated by the author: no phonetic (acoustic) evidence of stress, only segmental asymmetry.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem within the word (prefix unstressed, stem-initial syllable prominent); based on elicited words and sentences from Eboo speakers (Plateaux, Congo-Brazzaville); tonal melodies described over stem + following prefix.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2017 thesis describes Teke-Eboo (Boo/Eboo, B74b) as spoken on the Plateaux of Congo-Brazzaville, with Eboo speakers as consultants; the same author's 2012 paper argues Eboo and Nzikou are phonologically a single variety, matching Glottolog's languoid teke1278 'Teke-Eboo-Nzikou' [ebo]. The stress analysis is explicitly modelled on Paulian's description of neighbouring Teke-Kukuya (kuku1285) and Ngungwel (ngun1271), but the deciding statements quoted are the author's own first-hand claims about Eboo data.

new_statements.quote: This overview of consonant and vowel inventories shows a significant contrast between first and second syllables in stems, with a greatly reduced subset of consonants and vowels in the latter. Thus Eboo has 'stronger' or more robust stem-initial syllables compared to other syllables, just like Kukuya, suggesting that a stem-initial stress accent is preventing weakening or deletion of the more complex forms such as NCG sequences and long nasal vowels which only occur in initial syllables. [p.17] ... the lexical tone contrast is marked on the stem-initial mora, giving it prominence as the stressed syllable [p.18] ... There is nothing in the Eboo pitch graphs to indicate that stem-initial consonants or vowels are more intense, have a higher pitch, or are phonetically any different from consonants and vowels in other syllables. [p.68]

new_statements.reading: Teke-Eboo is a H/L tone language; word 'stress' is a fixed stem-initial (root-initial) prominence, never on prefixes, diagnosed only from segmental asymmetry (full C/V inventory restricted to the stem-initial syllable) and from the stem-initial mora carrying the lexical tone contrast on verbs. No acoustic correlate (intensity, pitch) was found, and the author herself prefers the label 'stem-initial prominence' over 'stress accent'. For catalog purposes: tone language with morphologically fixed stem-initial prominence, evidence segmental not phonetic; a coding as 'stress' should be flagged as inferred/weak.
